column2: Olson, teaching since 1948, formally takes on the rectorship in 1954, in the midst of an intense and lasting crisis touching every aspect of his life (erotic, domestic, poetic, pedagogical). An acute distrust, close to bitter hatred, of official institutions; a desire for a kind of refuge and solidarity
In the fall of 1954, his relationship with Betty Kaiser, a 28-year-old music student of Stefan Wolpe's, produces a child.

The fall 1954 issue publishes a fifteen-page sequence: prose by Lippman to open, Duncan's “Letters for Denise Levertov: An A Muse Ment,” two poems by the student Tom Field, Creeley's “The Whip,” Levertov's “Something,” and Creeley's preface to the portfolio of photographs by Peter Mitchum taken in a small French town in 1952, followed by “A Dilemma” signed R.C. Issues 1-4: 64 pages each, covers with geometric patterns by Kitasona Katue in homage to Albers; from issue 5 on, a fat annual format with scuffed covers bearing neither title nor table of contents Consequences: “The Whip” will go into The New American Poetry (1960) and For Love (1962).

Influenced by the Goodman brothers' Communitas (1947), the Williamses buy nearly a hundred acres of rural hillside and found a cooperative (not a commune) to refine the lessons of BMC. The site, called “the Land,” still exists. The first building: Karen Karnes and David Weinrib's ceramics studio, whose functional pieces provided the community with key income. Nearly 100 acres of sloping hillside; an Italian-style village around a square, most of the land left free and wild; terraced houses with open spaces Consequences: The creation of a home for the interdisciplinary practices of postwar American art and craft

A handwritten document in ink, “Plan for the Operation of Black Mountain College after 1956,” kept in the Olson archives at the University of Connecticut: proof that Olson was working on a plan for the college's survival beyond 1956. A sheet 8.5 x 11 inches, ink on paper Consequences: The college will close in 1957 despite this plan

Life publishes a photo story by Feininger, “Wife Coordinates Her Statues with Her Babies”; the sculpture Expectation (renamed Maternity) completed in nine months, like a pregnancy; captions reducing art to motherhood (a subject suggested by her 4-year-old daughter; First Born made after the second baby). Expectation/Maternity (1955); three children; nine months of work. Consequences: The mother-artist's work reduced to her motherhood.

City ordinances lead to slot machines being thrown out; Asawa salvages their colored wire and works it into her first sculptures. Colored wire from discarded slot machines Consequences: A signature material of her sculptural beginnings in San Francisco

Expecting their first child, Asawa turns a Japanese bamboo suitcase into a cradle and sews a mattress pad and a sheet from discarded bedding and a Navy blanket. Bamboo suitcase, U.S. Navy blanket, salvaged bedding
A self-organized exhibition by four women artist-craftsmen, centered on so-called feminine techniques. Consequences: The assertion of a position between art and craft

Despite the neutral title, four women exhibit: Dean's woven textiles, Wildenhain's ceramics, Renk's jewelry, Asawa's wire sculptures; the critic Alfred Frankenstein tries to classify the “wire things.” Frankenstein: “a form of knitting with iron and copper… very like the technique employed by medieval armorers”; some pieces are abstractions of trees, of coral Consequences: The discourse of gendered craft takes hold in Asawa's reception
Helps Taylor put on a recital of seven dances; for Resistance, he uses a dog that barks on cue at the beginning and end of the dance. A dog trained to bark on cue
The painter Jack Tworkov introduces Rauschenberg's work to the art dealer Charles Egan. Consequences: A first solo show at Egan's
Cornell's box assemblages are shown alongside works by Twombly at the Stable Gallery; Rauschenberg photographs the exhibition

Rauschenberg's financial situation stabilizes when he and Johns, now friends, begin dressing windows for Tiffany and Bonwit Teller Store windows for Tiffany and Bonwit Teller Consequences: Financial stability

Rauschenberg moves to a new studio on Pearl Street; Johns, also a Southerner, becomes his neighbor; they become inseparable Pearl Street studio Consequences: The beginning of five years of shared life and work

He begins to reveal surfaces of newspaper and incorporate found objects, art reproductions, and constructed appendages (Untitled, Collection, Charlene), the first Combine paintings, still mostly red; he coins the term “Combine” for painting-sculpture. Works still mostly red

An interview in Paris in which Duchamp sets out his notion of retinal painting: since Impressionism, painting stops at the retina and neglects the gray matter; he credits Surrealism with having tried to get rid of retinal content. Duchamp had been living in New York since 1942; a striking absence of Dada from his list Consequences: Breton appropriates the idea right after publication; Jouffroy will use it for Rauschenberg

Voulkos accepts the invitation to create a ceramics department; there he thinks of clay as art and not as craft, another way of inventing form; the studios are open 24 hours a day, with much night work, parties, music, and firings, a liberating and ambitious atmosphere, the line between teachers and students blurred. Studios open day and night, nighttime firings. Consequences: The birth of a major ceramics movement; Otis as heir to Richards's call at Black Mountain to take the training of craftsmen out of the classrooms into the bracing winds of life.

Around the mid-1950s, many Black Mountain students (Joe Fiore in particular) respond wholeheartedly to de Kooning and the New York Expressionists, embodying the New York spirit. Consequences: A young artist who had studied with de Kooning, Kline, or Tworkov had a potential mentor to contact in New York

The book is published by the University of Chicago Press, with international copyright; Goodman dedicates the work to four of his teachers and sets out in it his method of formal analysis of literature. Copyright 1954, set and printed in Chicago; distributed by Cambridge University Press (London) and the University of Toronto Press
Sells a large group of paintings to Martha Jackson; some are shown in her gallery (opened in 1953), others resold to West Coast dealers and shown in Los Angeles.

The family leaves Florida for Montgomery County, near Washington. Dikka joins the county library system and the library school at Catholic University; she becomes a branch librarian, bringing in a steady income and a constant flow of books for her voracious reader of a husband. Consequences: Financial stability at last.
The student Betty Kaiser gives birth to Olson's son in New York; he commutes; his wife eventually leaves Black Mountain; the student and the son join him.

The de Koonings share the house with Franz Kline and Ludwig Sander. For the big croquet party, Willem paints outhouse seats as decorations; Elaine makes crepe paper flowers, hangs them on the trees, and perfumes them. Painted outhouse seats, crepe paper flowers sprayed with perfume Consequences: Years later the forgotten seats, acquired by an East End art lover, were put up for sale as paintings, stirring up a controversy over their value

In an exceptionally cold winter and with no overcoat, Rumaker buys the cheapest one possible, a supposed “French import” in gray, with a wide belt and a big flared collar, which Ben judges at least stylish. $18, poor-quality fabric, does not survive the winter
Back in Ulm for New Year's, he continues his visits to cathedrals in Freiburg, Strasbourg, and Augsburg.

After all this news, Anni, fearful and always protective, writes that she hopes he is not doing too much and wearing himself out; a week later she repeats it: he should say NO sometimes, what with the parties, the finishing touches, the goodbyes, the packing, the boat, and the official report to hand in.

Elaine, Bill, and Kline paint a coconut and two grapefruits into softballs so convincing that Rosenberg pitches them one by one to Pavia, who swings with full force, at fruit, to general laughter. Atmosphere: The artists' collective giggles, a spirit of farce.

Every evening, Robert brings Olson home to dinner; the giant arrives in a fresh white shirt, savors Helen's French cooking; little is said about Europe, almost absent from his orbit; he lays out his idea of American space Atmosphere: Warm but lopsided: the young European outside the poet's great orbit Stakes: A meeting of two worldviews: the contained Mediterranean against maximal American space

End of summer: the whole college, both company and audience, performs Wolpe's opera after Ibsen; Hellman sings Peer, Olson takes on the roles of the Great Boyg and the Button Molder; at rehearsals, Stefan lingers at the keyboard and regretfully gives up song and piano Atmosphere: A collective celebration and the melancholy of the pianist leaving his keyboard Stakes: The dying college turns itself into theater

After weeks of rehearsing Uncle Vanya (at which Stefan Wolpe weeps), Huss works on scenes from Ghosts; Helen, as Mrs. Alving, feels her voice change and her gestures become those of a mother discovering the syphilis passed by the father to her son, played by Rumaker Atmosphere: An intimate revelation of the actor's metamorphosis Stakes: Theater as passage into another body

Creeley, after a night's drive from New York, knocks at Olson's door; it is opened by a mountain of a man wrapped in a towel, otherwise naked, who urges him in; breakfast, conversation; Olson asks whether he is ready; Creeley would like a day or two to settle in; Olson draws him along, and that same evening Creeley is standing in front of a class. Words: Olson urges him to come in, then asks whether he is ready to go; Creeley would have liked a day or two to settle in. Atmosphere: Unbridled warmth, sweeping energy Stakes: The immediate initiation of a man who has never taught

Six students huddled at one end of the immense table; Creeley alone at the other, staring at the wall, dabbing his streaming eye (the patch left behind); a grave, rasping, inaudible monologue; Karen Karnes asks him to speak up; his voice rises for a few minutes, then falls again. Words: Karen Karnes asks whether he can speak louder. Atmosphere: Solemn embarrassment, physical unease Stakes: The botched baptism of a teacher who became legendary

Gerry surprises Stone with a box planted with seeds and divided by a partition; Stone explains that he is sowing both sides, concentrating good thoughts on one side and bad ones on the other, to see which grows better. Words: Gerry asks Grey Stone what he is doing; Stone: seeds on both sides of the partition, good thoughts on one side, bad ones on the other. Atmosphere: Stony seriousness, rustic mysticism

Creeley, in his verbal cruelty, teases one of the women; she gets up and walks toward him smiling, a lit cigarette aimed at his good eye; it is he who backs off. Atmosphere: A smile and a threat Stakes: The limits of words against action

Field is driving; the others tease him about his penchant for playing the fool, Creeley hammering home in his soft, relentless voice that he must give up the pretense of incompetence; Field tries to shut them up, fails, floors the accelerator, and flies toward the big stone wall. Words: Field: “All right, you bastards, this is what you want” Atmosphere: Contained hysteria, then an explosion Stakes: The community's volatility pushed to its peak

Rumaker is climbing up from the hills toward evening; Olson comes out in town clothes with a suitcase, followed by Connie with a pinched look. Olson opens the trunk, sees Rumaker, freezes, smiles sheepishly, turns around, finger to his gray mustache with a “shh,” and goes back in; Connie runs ahead of him. Rumaker stays planted in the dusty road, giving up crossing their yard out of respect. Words: No words; total silence in the scene; only the pantomime of the “shh” Atmosphere: Late afternoon, dust, unease, secrets Stakes: Will Olson leave Connie and the college for Betty and his son in New York?

Rumaker, alone, is thinking about his tutorials; Connie appears without a sound, like a wild animal, apologizes for disturbing him, sits down, and lights a cork-tipped king-size cigarette, her fingers trembling. A long silence; she looks around: “It's so quiet here”. Rumaker says something banal; she decides to say nothing, relaxes, and leaves. He regrets not having been able to reach out for her hand, a distance as far as the moon. Words: “I hope I'm not bothering you”; “It's so quiet here” Atmosphere: Smoke as thin as a sigh, an imaginary breeze, Connie's naked courage, Rumaker's helplessness Stakes: Will Connie be able to speak of her pain? No: the scene stays suspended

At dusk, Rumaker holds the flashlight; Tom, crouching and on the alert like a wild animal, plunges his hand into the mud and pulls out enormous bullfrogs, killing them with a jab of the point of the butcher knife inherited from his father, a tugboat cook; back to Meadows Inn, breading, frying on the Coleman. Atmosphere: Dusk, mud, hunger, and joyful ingenuity Stakes: The material survival of the dying college

One evening, Olson reads Douglas Woolf's “The Kind of Life We've Planned” (sent by Creeley); the class, led by Dorn and Fick, snubs it; Olson, the only one who understands what Woolf was doing, chews them out collectively for their obtuseness; general amazement at his praise for a story about middle-class golfers. Words: Verbal scorn for a “love story” about middle-class golfers hitting a little white ball Atmosphere: Hilarity turned into a collective slap Stakes: What may one read and write? Olson against clique prejudice

Tea served in more or less intact cups, chairs carefully arranged, Olson's plea for a school where Black and white would study together (mention of Jacob Lawrence, 1946); suddenly Kate, naked, dragging a dead bird by the wing, followed by baby David Huss, just as naked; the minister exclaims, Kate answers with her four-letter word, the wife is shocked; Olson, crestfallen, tries to salvage things. Words: “Oh! What happened to the poor bird?” — “The fuckin' owl did it.” Atmosphere: Black comedy in a bucolic setting; the college's curse in action. Stakes: The failure of the last chance to recruit Black students, through the very Edenic innocence of the place.

Rumaker, perched on the tall stepladder, wipes the windows; a visitor arrives; Olson introduces him; Rumaker calls down, “I'm the houseboy!”; Olson smiles back, barely annoyed. Words: Rumaker: “I'm the houseboy!” Atmosphere: A budding complicity between master and student Stakes: A measure of Rumaker's new confidence in Olson

After the party and the ride in the Hillman Minx, naked on the white sand under the moon; Rumaker, drunk, imagines hill people lying in wait, panics, and insists on going back; Williams, exasperated, gives in and takes him back to Streamside. Words: Rumaker: too dangerous; they must go back, where it is safe. Atmosphere: Ash-white sand, pressing trees, the sudden terror of the hidden eye Stakes: The fear of desire between men and of the rural gaze

Baker, sitting at the back, accuses Olson of making the students believe they are great; Olson draws himself up, stares at her, and invokes Dostoevsky; she holds firm, and he explodes in a hoarse voice: “I'm dynamite!”; Rumaker squirms on his cane chair. Words: Baker: they should not be led to believe they are great. Olson: the aim is to create Dostoevskys; “I'm tough, don't mess with me—I'm dynamite!” Atmosphere: Rage, embarrassment, torn loyalties Stakes: Olson's authority challenged on his own ground

After the desertions to the Roxy, Olson, agitated, cuts a pane and slices open his thumb; he stares at the blood, crying “Look at that!”; Rumaker thinks of the line from Marlowe quoted in class and of his father burned by matches; Olson goes off to have Connie bandage him; everyone takes off for the Roxy in Tom's Buick. Words: Olson: “Look at that! Look at that!”; Marlowe: “See, see, where Christ's blood streams in the firmament!” Atmosphere: Blood, stupefaction, general desertion Stakes: The leader wounded, authority collapses in a minute

In a viciously gleeful attack on Slater Brown, Olson acts out the scene: he mimics Crane's bathetic tears as he begs Brown to come back from another man Words: “O please come back, Slater—Puh-lease come back!”, a melodramatic wail Atmosphere: Fits of laughter; Olson an excellent comic actor Stakes: The master's possible homophobia; Rumaker will later check that there are no tear stains on the letters

Sober, Jackson climbs the stairs and joins Bill in front of an old television set; Bill spends hours in silence before old movies, especially westerns and musicals, while Jackson picks fights when he is drunk Atmosphere: Television silence, an interior sheltered from sand and sun Stakes: A fragile complicity between two rivals

The Brookses see cars along the street and invite themselves in. In the yard: wheelbarrows of hard-boiled eggs, abundant food; Elaine climbs into the trees to spray cologne on the hundreds of crepe paper flowers she has fastened there; Bill has painted the outhouse seats and laid out the croquet. Words: Charlotte Brooks: “wheelbarrows full of hard-boiled eggs… and a lot of wonderful food” Atmosphere: Summer, irreverent gaiety, an in-group Stakes: The last carefree summers before the couple's breakup

After a series of farewell parties, the students accompany Albers to the train and send him off to the sound of a trumpet fanfare. Atmosphere: Collective fervor, a resounding farewell. Stakes: The imprint left by a teacher.

With the dining hall closed and the buildings unheated, Olson types on onionskin paper a diagram of concentric circles: “The College” at the center, then theater, academy, magazine, and publishing house spread out as far as Berkeley, Cambridge, New York, Philadelphia, and San Francisco; under North Carolina at the center: “mytho-, archaeo-, bio-, geo-”. Atmosphere: Despair transmuted into a dream of fruitful dispersal, a dream image of a cosmopolitan college. Stakes: Saving through atomization what the dying place can no longer carry.
An interview whose last words by Duchamp, much quoted, give their meaning to the title Anti-Procès (“Down with Moral Judgements”) Words: “The idea of judgement should disappear”

In an interview, Duchamp unrolls his genealogy of modern art: Impressionism, Fauvism, Cubism, abstraction, all retinal, and rehabilitates Surrealism for having tried to escape it Words: “Impressionism, Fauvism, Cubism, abstraction, it's always retinal painting” Stakes: A theory that will cross the Atlantic and be used again for Rauschenberg

An exchange of letters on the future of the department; Albers suggests as successors Gyorgy Kepes, Raymond Dowden, perhaps George L.K. Morris, Thomas Folds, or Wilhelmus B. Bryan Mandatory retirement at 68; a post accepted for six years

Shows a Black Painting and a “Grass Painting” made of soil sown with seed and watered until it sprouted; the only surviving example dies of cold in the Fulton Street studio. Soil, seeds, watering; death by cold

In late winter 1954, Elaine writes to Larry Rivers with evident relief that she is working on her very last technical article, on Balcomb Greene, and is leaving the “X Paints a Picture” series for broader themes. Consequences: A turn toward the criticism of ideas (“Subject: What, How, or Who?”, 1955)

On a work break away from Black Mountain, Rumaker roams Crane's Bowery of the 1890s, looking for traces; the setting of “An Experiment in Misery” is still there; he also thinks of Maxwell Bodenheim, the bohemian poet of the 1920s, later murdered there with his third wife by a former mental patient. The girders of the elevated; Crane had disguised himself as a bum for two weeks, begging, drinking in the rotgut bars, and sleeping in the flops.

Despite several recent strokes, Williams reads his poems in a flat, slow voice, apologizing for slurred words and explaining his speech therapy; on poetic composition and the variable foot, his voice becomes passionate and fire comes into his eyes; at the signing, Rumaker, too shy to talk to him about Olson and Black Mountain, stares at him from close up, and Williams gives him a slight, questioning smile. A brown suit, a thin brown face, very dark brown eyes; one of his sons, a doctor, stands protectively beside him during the signing; a packed hall

Arrived from Black Mountain a few days earlier with no place to stay, they sleep at night locked in Herb's old 1939 Ford, packed to the roof, and look for lodgings by day; they have colds and are exhausted. Consequences: They ask Rumaker to put them up

The first night: after their first showers in days, Merrill and Herb in their sleeping bags a few feet from Rumaker's mattress; believing him asleep, they unzip and make love; Rumaker, wild with rage, starts coughing as loudly as he can until it all stops, then lies rigid, fists clenched, grinding his teeth. The wind whistling through the rattling windows Consequences: The next day they find a loft on Rivington Street

They find a huge, cheap loft, a former factory space in the old Jewish neighborhood, to be fixed up, full of windows, many of them broken; they sleep there in their sleeping bags while making it livable. Consequences: The end of their stay at Rumaker's

Mary Ann leaves the place on Minetta Lane to live with Seymour on West 12th Street, leaving Rumaker unable to pay the rent alone. $60 rent plus utilities against a salary of $48 a week Consequences: Rumaker looks for a cheaper room

Drawn by a “Room for Rent” sign, Rumaker is questioned by a frail old Southern lady with hennaed hair and a ruffled gauze dress, who asks whether he likes opera; she trusts only opera lovers, insists that the door always be locked, and points out a resident upstairs who has a life on another street; a tiny room, a narrow bed, a small armchair, no radiator, only a heating pipe, a stuffy smell, but the tugboat horns on the Hudson can be heard. $4 a week, clean linen once a week, rent expected on time Consequences: Rumaker moves in with his trunk shipped by rail freight from the college, wasting $2 on a taxi

Fiore and Field having come to New York on business, Rumaker pays his share of the gas and rides back to the college in Joe Fiore's Jeep station wagon. A contribution to the gas; a Jeep station wagon; crossing the pine-covered foothills of North Carolina at dusk Consequences: Back to the college for the spring 1954 term

The morning after his return, Rumaker walks around the campus, setting down each step with gratitude; he touches daffodils piercing the snow along the Lake Eden path. Late February air with a raw hint of spring; patches of snow; clumps of bright daffodils

Rumaker settles into Meadows Inn with Tom Field and Terence Burns, awaiting Creeley's arrival and copies of the first issue of the Black Mountain Review. Each has his own room; the three share the whole second floor.

Howe reaches the mandatory age of 68 and retires from the chairmanship of the Department of Architecture; students and teachers give him one of Albers's Structural Constellation engravings on laminated plastic. An engraving on laminated plastic; the mandatory age of 68

In March 1954, Rauschenberg and Johns see the exhibition Magritte: Word Vs. Image at Sidney Janis; according to some, Gablik introduced the two artists to each other shortly before or after; in an interview, she does not remember her role. Consequences: Rauschenberg will acquire Magritte's The Proper Image IV (1929).

A packed hall; Williams alone onstage, in a brown suit, reads slowly, apologizes for his slurring, explains his therapy; when he comes to measure and the variable foot, the fire rises to his eyes and throat, and he gestures; afterward, in the lobby, his doctor son beside him, he signs with a slowed hand, kind to everyone; Rumaker works his way to the wall a few feet from the table, wants to utter the names of Olson and Black Mountain, but dares not; Williams catches him staring and gives him a slight, questioning smile before another book is set down. Words: Williams says he has taken speech therapy to learn to speak distinctly again Atmosphere: Painful fragility and a miracle of presence; the young admirer's unspeakable excitement Stakes: The wounded master passing on the torch; shyness that prevents speech

After their first showers in days, Merrill and Herb settle into sleeping bags a few feet from the mattress; Rumaker, awake in the dark, hears the zippers and the quickening breathing; seething with rage, he starts coughing, fake hacking louder and louder, until there is silence and the zippers close again; then he lies rigid, teeth clenched, coughing now and then as a warning, satisfied at having deprived Merrill of his pleasure, before sinking into sleep. Atmosphere: Darkness, wind at the windows, smothered resentment, the unwitting comedy of the cough Stakes: A spurned lover's tiny revenge under his own roof

The door opens only a crack; the lady, with a soft Southern accent, asks whether Rumaker wants a little room, then, inexplicably, whether he likes opera; when he says yes, she smiles, unlocks the door, confides that one can always trust someone who likes opera, insists that the door be locked at all times, murmurs that all the young men in the house adore opera, and points out a woman upstairs who has a life on another street; then the climb up the dark hallway to the tiny room with the heating pipe. Words: “I know I can always trust someone who likes opera”; “It's four dollars a week” Atmosphere: A zany and unsettling closed world, stuffiness, whispers, mustiness Stakes: Finding a roof at a pittance; the comedy of codes among insiders

Rumaker falls asleep in the Jeep station wagon and wakes at dusk: an enormous black bird with great flapping wings comes down in the middle of the road ahead of them and rips open with its sharp beak a small wild creature twitching on the asphalt. Atmosphere: Dusk in the pines, a shiver, a haunting image Stakes: A dire omen that will become a delirious reality more than a year later (flash-forward)

In the early morning after his return, Rumaker walks around the campus, setting each foot down with cautious gratitude; he bends to touch the daffodils piercing the snow; he knew he was back where he belonged. Atmosphere: The raw air of late February already tinged with spring, joy Stakes: The college as a home regained at the very moment it is dying

She writes that every day she has a new idea proving that every painting she has done was all wrong; she calls this state disorganized energy and prefers it to organized energy, which leads only to money, creating bigger and more annoying problems. In 1955, a teaching job having fallen through, she looks for another way to make money without spending time on it

His marriage in crisis, desperate to leave Majorca, Creeley, who had never taught or really held a job, arrives at 8 a.m. after an all-night drive from New York in a 1940 pickup. He knocks at Olson's door: a first meeting with a mountain of a man, naked under a towel, who warmly invites him in. After breakfast, Olson draws him in: that same evening Creeley is in front of a class. A 1940 pickup; 8 a.m.; Olson naked under a bath towel; “Well, are you ready to go?”; his wife had cabled him: “If you just can't do it, by all means simply come back.” Consequences: A very mixed start in teaching; the worst first class (the conference room of the Studies Building, an immense table, six students).
A text sent to alumni, friends, and foundations couples a request for money with a plan for expansion: a new faculty and the hiring of an “Administrative Secretary” for administrative affairs.

The only letter he ever received from his father: a brief note in pencil, in the neat hand of a parochial schoolboy on lined paper, announcing the birth of David, the ninth child, when his mother was 48 and Dr. Campo had assured her she was past menopause; his father, drunk, will call the child Dr. Campo's son or the priest's son Pencil, lined notebook paper, March 1954, mother aged 48, ninth child, Dr. Campo with a cigarillo and a fat roll of bills in his pocket, a reconciliation through the parish priest Consequences: Rumaker's anger at Campo, the priest, and his father; the poverty of the 1930s resurfacing; for weeks, the sight of a pregnant woman makes him want to hit her in the belly

In the spring of 1954, Rumaker moves in with Terence Burns and Tom Field on the lower floor of Meadows Inn, Natasha and Eric's (Goldowski) former apartment. Natasha and Eric's former apartment; separate kitchens required

Olson and Creeley, who had never met despite years of correspondence, spend their first hours together on the bench in Olson's yard; Rumaker, who has gone to borrow sugar from the Husses, finds them there and is introduced. Creeley in a dark blue beret, a patch over one eye, loose work clothes; Olson puts his big arm around Creeley's shoulder; Creeley has driven nonstop from New York to North Carolina in his battered old pickup. Consequences: Creeley gets to work that same evening.

After a few classes, the class moves into Olson's favorite little Reading Room (warm, draft-free), better suited to Creeley's intimate style; no more complaints of inaudibility. Consequences: Creeley gains confidence and becomes an effective teacher.

Creeley, arriving at 8 a.m. in a 1940 pickup after driving all night, knocks at Olson's door. Olson, a mountain of a man naked under a towel, warmly invites him in. Breakfast, conversation, then Olson: “Well, are you ready to go?” Creeley would like to settle in for a day or two; Olson draws him in, and that same evening Creeley teaches his first class. Words: Olson: “come in, come in,” then “Well, are you ready to go?”; Creeley's wife had cabled: “If you just can't do it, by all means simply come back.” Atmosphere: Dawn after a night on the road; Olson's disheveled warmth, joyful urgency Stakes: A life turned upside down: a man with no job and no experience thrown into teaching within twelve hours

On the very evening of his arrival, Creeley finds himself in front of six students grouped around an immense table that fills the room. Atmosphere: Embarrassment, clutter, a botched start Stakes: The myth of the charismatic master against the reality of chaotic teaching (“this was Black Mountain not Hollywood”)

One morning, on his way out, Rumaker sees the tall grass rippling with no wind: it is a rattlesnake that, alerted by the door and the footsteps, is sliding toward the pinewood. Atmosphere: A brief tension in the morning calm Stakes: A wild confirmation of being at home

Rumaker, coming back with his bag of sugar from the Husses, sees Olson and a stranger in a blue beret and an eye patch sitting very close together on the bench; Olson is speaking gravely into Creeley's ear, and Creeley listens with his head down; Rumaker means to pass by with a greeting, but Olson calls him over and introduces him; the bag of sugar awkwardly switched from his right hand to his left; a handshake; small talk; Creeley's eye starts streaming, and he wipes it with quick dabs. Words: Olson, with a radiant smile, calls Michael over to meet Robert Creeley; he adds, as a guarantee, that Rumaker will be in his writing class, which panics the young man. Atmosphere: Late-morning March light; mutual embarrassment and immediate sympathy; Rumaker's shame at his stupid brown bag. Stakes: The first meeting of the shy apprentice and the shy master; the recognition of a shared vulnerability.

On the very evening of his arrival, Creeley, without his eye patch, alone at one end of the big table, stares at the wall, wiping his streaming eye; an inaudible monologue; Karen Karnes asks him to speak up; he does so for a few minutes, then falls back; he asks desperately whether anyone has brought writing; Rumaker reads two entries from his New York journal; Creeley receives them favorably. Words: Karnes asks whether he can speak louder; Creeley asks whether anyone has brought any writing, perhaps, he fears, with the opposite hope that someone has. Atmosphere: Unease and compassion; the eye streaming buckets under the emotion. Stakes: The celebrated poet, helpless before six students: the birth of a teaching.

Paintings and drawings from the last five years; Betty Parsons, visited earlier, had said nothing (Hedda Sterne will later tell her that Parsons would have taken her on if she had followed up); it is her former teacher Marca-Relli who steers her to Eleanor Ward; the gallery, set up in a former stable, still smells of horses. Consequences: She will always advise young artists to get sponsored by an artist connected with a gallery

An early still life, a portrait of Fairfield Porter, basketball players, abstractions including Event in a Warehouse (perhaps linked to the deadly warehouse explosions in Muncie, Plains, Wilmington, Rosine, and Houston in 1953) and Sympathizer (perhaps a response to McCarthyism); prices from $30 (a drawing) to $700; Stuart Preston (New York Times) attacks her pugnacious brushstrokes but admires her drawing and her genial vitality, spoiled by consistently drab color; Fairfield Porter (ARTnews) hails her incisive wit and portraits both sympathetic and frighteningly sharp, concluding that hers is a stubborn and astute personality.

Elaine often claimed that her first solo show dated from 1952; it took place in April 1954 at the Stable Gallery, founded in 1953. The exact date was established from the chronology by her sister Marjorie Luyckx
Back for the spring of 1954, Rumaker reads aloud selected passages from his notebook in Creeley's first writing class. A notebook kept daily during the New York winter

After long postponements, Creeley sees Rumaker to talk about his writing: Rumaker finds him hanging his laundry (including tattered Jockey shorts) on a sagging line under the open floor; a tropical storm breaks, the rain blows in under the ground floor; in the apartment, the rain comes in through the windows left open and around a piece of cardboard plugging a broken pane; Creeley rushes to close the windows and gather up papers set on the sill. Creeley may have just been wrestling with the secondhand automatic washing machine in the former chemistry lab, which bucks on the concrete floor and has to be ridden at the risk of electrocution; “temporary” wooden stairs dating from the construction of the 1940s.

The soprano aria from Act III wins one of the three prizes of the Twentieth Century Masterpiece Festival at La Musica nel XX Secolo, a festival sponsored by the Congress for Cultural Freedom; the performance is noticed by Leontyne Price. 2,500 Swiss francs; a festival funded by the Farfield Foundation, later revealed as a CIA front. Consequences: Harrison, presumably without knowing it, passively contributes to the cultural Cold War; he then leaves for the West Coast and Indonesian music.

An exhibition in a single gallery according to Lanier's arrangement: Asawa's wire sculptures hanging from the skylit ceiling, Wildenhain's pottery on raised platforms, Dean's textiles hung on the walls, Renk's jewelry in built-in cases, one of them suspended by four cables floating in the center, behind a curved entrance wall bearing the four names in black sans serif type. Photographer: Bob Hall; letters of congratulation from Morley to Lanier. Consequences: A counter-model to the identity of the “designer-craftsman” in the service of industry.

Rumaker, coming up from the library by the shortcut through the tall grass, surprises Creeley hanging his laundry (tattered shorts) on a sagging line; a look of embarrassment, then anger, in Creeley's single eye, his body dodging with jerks of the shoulder; a tropical storm breaks; they climb the temporary stairs; in the apartment, the rain comes in through the open windows and around the cardboard in the broken pane; Creeley rushes over, slams the windows, gathers up little papers lined up on the sill. Words: No words reported: Creeley's body speaks for him, caught between obligation and flight. Atmosphere: Sheets of rain, an empty corridor of closed doors, an almost empty apartment; Creeley's nervous tension, his heart in Majorca. Stakes: The promised master slips away: the meeting about writing comes down to a domestic flight in the downpour.

The A&P grocery heir and collector publishes a full page titled “The Public Be Damned?” in most of the major American newspapers, attacking modern art and singling out de Kooning. A full-page letter in most of the major newspapers, May 1954 Consequences: Gives Bill national publicity; his reputation does not suffer
In early June, the housemates go to fetch crates of books from the booksellers Carol and Don Braider (who also showed the artists' paintings) to store in the basement of the Red House.

In early June, Elaine's housemates go to fetch crates of books from the booksellers Carol and Don Braider for the basement of the Red House. Pollock, already drunk, arrives in his Model A Ford and drinks a few more beers. Nervous at being alone with him (according to one account, he started chasing her around the house), she calls the bookstore to hurry the men back. While horsing around with them on a crumbling path behind the house, Pollock trips, Bill falls on him, and breaks his ankle. Model A Ford, beers, a crumbling path behind the back door, a broken ankle Consequences: The rivalry between the two artists turns this minor accident into a cause célèbre, one of the three memorable events of that boozy summer.

The following summer, an abstract ink drawing made in Vicente's class, pinned up as a joke in the lobby of Meadows Inn, where Tom Field and Rumaker live, among Tom's drawings, catches the attention of Joe Fiore, who compliments it. An improvised show for visitors Consequences: Precious praise from Joe

After the spring term in June 1954, fired by Jonathan Williams's tales of the French Quarter (jazz clubs, the clarinetist George Lewis), Rumaker and Field set out hitchhiking for ~500 miles, planning ~5 days with friends of Jonathan's. Jonathan first drives them in his English Hillman Minx to Highlands, to his parents' house, the parents being away, where they sleep. A dark brown imitation-crocodile suitcase sent by Rumaker's mother through her Yellow Savings Stamps; Tom gets by on the GI Bill after his service as a stretcher-bearer in Korea; Rumaker has saved for weeks; Friday morning, Jonathan in a black corduroy jacket, a red Abercrombie & Fitch hunting shirt, a black suede cap, and chinos; the little Hillman has to be pushed over several Blue Ridge crests. Consequences: Rumaker becomes aware of the Deep South and its dangers.

A comfortable pine-paneled ranch house, pine furniture upholstered in beige tartan; Jonathan proudly shows his room with its shelves of books and records, then the spectacular view of the deep purple Great Smoky Mountains, from which three states can be seen (Georgia, Tennessee, South Carolina), which he names in his soft Southern voice with the proprietary air of a lord of the manor.

Saturday morning, the first ride: a skinny trio of young drunks still debauched from the night before, banging on the sides of their old Chevy and letting out deafening rebel yells; the red-haired, red-faced driver speeds along bumpy roads. They invent a pretext to get out at a crossroads; the car takes off in a cloud of dust.

Late Saturday afternoon, starving, they eat a good hot meal in a back-street “greasy spoon”; then they take a city bus to the outskirts to avoid the difficulties of hitchhiking in town, the police, and the risk of being arrested as vagrants and sent to the chain gang. Atlanta seen from the bus at dusk: old houses, neat lawns, tree-lined streets; Rumaker thinks of Peachtree Street, Vivien Leigh's Scarlett O'Hara, and Butterfly McQueen's Prissy.
